mod_01.text:
You receive an email saying:

"Your school account will be deleted today. Verify now."

Which detail is the strongest warning sign?
options: The email mentions your school
It contains your name
It creates urgency to make you act quickly
It was sent in the morning
mod_01.explanation: The threat of losing the account today puts you under pressure to click before you can check whether the school sent the message.

options: Pretending to be trustworthy through messages to steal information or cause an unsafe action
Physically stealing someone's device
Guessing passwords automatically
Blocking access to a website
mod_01.explanation: Phishing uses a trusted identity to persuade someone to act. The attacker may want a password, a download, or a payment.

mod_01.text:
An email says it is from your university, but the sender is:

registrar.school@gmail.com

What should concern you most?
options: It contains "registrar"
It has no attachment
It contains your name
It uses Gmail rather than the school's expected official domain
mod_01.explanation: Anyone can put the school's name before the @ sign. The part after it is gmail.com, which differs from the school's expected domain.

mod_01.text: A suspicious email asks you to log in immediately. What is safest?
options: Click the email link
Open the official website yourself
Reply asking whether it is legitimate
Forward it to a friend first
mod_01.explanation: Opening the portal from a saved bookmark lets you check for an alert without using a link chosen by the sender.

options: https://school.edu.ph.login-verification.net
https://portal.school.edu.ph
https://school.edu.ph/login
https://library.school.edu.ph
mod_01.explanation: The site is under login-verification.net. Putting school.edu.ph at the beginning of that address makes it look familiar.

mod_01.text:
An email shows:

Display name: University Registrar
Actual address: studentverify247@gmail.com

What should you trust when checking the sender?
options: Display name
Profile photo
Actual email address and domain
Email signature
mod_01.explanation: A sender can copy the registrar's display name. Expand the address and compare its domain with the one in your school directory.

mod_01.text:
You hover over "Open Student Portal" and see:

https://school-login.secure-account.xyz

What should you do?
options: Open it because HTTPS is shown
Avoid it and access the portal independently
Open it in private browsing
Ask a friend to test it
mod_01.explanation: The link opens a page under secure-account.xyz. Using your saved portal address avoids sending your login to that destination.

mod_01.text:
An unexpected email contains:

ClassSchedule.pdf.exe

Why is this dangerous?
options: PDF files are unsafe
Long filenames cannot be trusted
School files should always be ZIP files
.exe indicates the file can execute a program
mod_01.explanation: Windows reads the last extension. In ClassSchedule.pdf.exe, opening the file can run a program even though its name suggests a PDF.

mod_01.text: Your instructor's real name appears in an email asking you to open a project document. What would make it most suspicious?
options: It references your real project
It uses correct grammar
The email comes from an unfamiliar domain
It contains the instructor's signature
mod_01.explanation: Compare the sender's domain with the saved school domain. Someone can copy your instructor's name and project details into an email from another domain.

mod_01.text: What is the best way to verify an unexpected request from your instructor?
options: Contact the instructor using a previously known channel
Reply to the suspicious email
Click the link to inspect it
Check whether the message uses the instructor's photo
mod_01.explanation: Calling a saved number or starting a new message to the instructor's school address lets you check with the instructor directly. Replying could reach the impersonator.

mod_01.text:
An email claiming to be IT support asks for your password.

What should you do?
options: Send it if the address looks official
Send only part of it
Change it and send the new password
Refuse and verify with IT independently
mod_01.explanation: Someone with your password could sign in as you. Use IT's published contact details to report the request and get help.

mod_01.text:
Consider:

https://accounts.school.edu.ph.security-check.com

Who controls the main registered domain?
options: school.edu.ph
security-check.com
accounts.school.edu.ph
accounts
mod_01.explanation: The address ends in security-check.com. The words accounts.school.edu.ph are subdomains chosen by whoever controls security-check.com.

mod_01.text: You clicked a phishing link and entered your password. What should you do next?
options: Delete the email
Restart the browser
Change the password using the legitimate site and report the incident
Wait to see whether anything happens
mod_01.explanation: The password may already be in someone else's hands. Changing it through the real site and alerting support gives them a chance to secure the account.

mod_01.text: Which provides the weakest evidence that an email is legitimate?
options: It uses the organization's logo and your real name
You independently confirmed the request with the sender
The domain matches the organization's official domain
The request appears inside an official account portal
mod_01.explanation: A logo can be copied, and a name can come from a class list. Neither shows who sent this particular email.

mod_01.text:
An email looks legitimate but asks you to urgently download confidential documents from an unfamiliar domain.

What should determine your decision?
options: How professional the email looks
Whether the action and destination can be independently verified
Whether it contains your correct name
Whether the attachment is small
mod_01.explanation: Use a known school contact to confirm both the request and where the file should come from. A convincing message can still point to the wrong site.

mod_02.text:
You receive this text:

"GCash Security: Your wallet has been locked. Tap the link below immediately to restore access."

What makes this most likely a smishing attempt?
options: It mentions a mobile wallet
It uses a message to pressure you into taking an action
It was received on a phone
It contains the word "Security"
mod_02.explanation: The locked-wallet warning creates fear and supplies its own link as the solution. Open your wallet app independently to check the alert.

mod_02.text:
A text claiming to be from your bank says:

"We detected an unauthorized payment. Reply with the 6-digit OTP we just sent so we can cancel it."

What should you do?
options: Send the OTP because you did not make the payment
Send only the first three digits
Ask the sender to prove they work for the bank
Do not send the OTP and verify through the bank's official channel
mod_02.explanation: An OTP can authorize a login or payment. Giving it to the sender could approve the very action they claim they will cancel.

mod_02.text:
You receive an unexpected delivery text containing a link to pay a small redelivery fee.

What is the safest first action?
options: Open the courier's official app or website yourself and check the tracking information
Open the link because the fee is small
Reply asking whether the message is real
Forward the link to someone else to test it
mod_02.explanation: A scammer can invent a delivery problem. Checking the tracking record in the courier's official app lets you verify whether a fee is actually due.

mod_02.text: Which message is the strongest example of smishing?
options: Your school app displays your normal class schedule
A courier app you already installed reports that your parcel was delivered
An unexpected SMS threatens to suspend your account unless you open a link
Your phone displays a low-battery warning
mod_02.explanation: Smishing uses text messages. Here the threat of suspension gives you a reason to tap an unexpected link before checking the account.

mod_02.text:
You receive:

"Your student allowance is ready. Confirm at bit.ly/student-pay before 5 PM."

Why should the link increase your suspicion?
options: All bit.ly links are malware
Short links cannot use encryption
Schools cannot send links by SMS
The shortened link hides the actual destination
mod_02.explanation: The short address shows the shortening service but hides the site it will open. The deadline gives you less time to check with the school.

mod_02.text:
A message begins:

"GCash Alert"

and uses the correct company name and logo.

What should you conclude?
options: The message is legitimate because the brand is correct
A familiar brand name alone does not prove the sender is legitimate
The message is legitimate if it arrived in the morning
Companies cannot be impersonated by text
mod_02.explanation: A sender can copy GCash's name and artwork into a text. Open the wallet app yourself to see whether it shows the same alert.

mod_02.text:
You receive:

"Your SIM will be disabled in 30 minutes. Verify at telecom-security-help.com."

What is the safest action?
options: Open the link but do not enter a password
Reply to the sender asking for more information
Contact your carrier through its official app, website, or known number
Ask a friend to open the link first
mod_02.explanation: The countdown pushes you toward a site named by the sender. Your carrier can confirm the status of your SIM through contact details you already trust.

mod_02.text:
Someone messages you from a new number:

"Hi, this is Mom. My phone broke. Please send ₱4,000 now."

What is the strongest way to verify the request?
options: Contact your mother through a previously trusted method or another trusted family member
Ask the sender to tell you your birthday
Send a smaller amount first
Ask for a photo
mod_02.explanation: A reply to the new number only reaches the person asking for money. Calling a saved number lets you check whether your mother actually made the request.

mod_02.text:
A text says:

"Your ₱6,800 charge becomes permanent in 10 minutes. Tap now for a refund."

What social-engineering technique is being used most clearly?
options: Encryption
Password cracking
Software installation
Urgency and fear of losing money
mod_02.explanation: A large possible loss and a ten-minute deadline make tapping feel urgent. Check the charge in your own banking app.

mod_02.text: Which message should you be most likely to report as suspicious?
options: "Your monthly pass renews tomorrow. View details in the app you already use."
"Your wallet is frozen. Send your OTP here within five minutes."
"Your parcel was delivered successfully."
"Your bookstore reservation is available for pickup at the counter."
mod_02.explanation: The sender wants an OTP in the same conversation that threatens to freeze the wallet. Reporting the request helps protect the account without giving away the code.

mod_02.text:
You receive:

"MetroRide refund: metro-ride-help.tk/refund"

The real company's known website is:

"metroride.ph"

What is the strongest warning sign?
options: The text uses the word "refund"
The message was sent by SMS
The destination uses a different domain from the company's known domain
The link contains a slash
mod_02.explanation: Metro-ride-help.tk and metroride.ph are different domains. A similar company name in a refund link does not establish who runs the site.

mod_02.text:
A message knows your full name, phone number, and the store where you recently made a purchase.

Does this prove the text is legitimate?
options: Yes, because scammers cannot know recent purchases
Yes, if your phone number is also correct
Only if the message has no spelling errors
No; personal information can be leaked, purchased, guessed, or obtained elsewhere
mod_02.explanation: A purchase detail can come from a leaked receipt or another source. Check the claim through the store's known contact channel.

mod_02.text:
Your school normally uses:

"westfield.edu"

Which link is most suspicious?
options: https://portal.westfield.edu
https://westfield.edu.verify-account.net
https://library.westfield.edu
https://westfield.edu
mod_02.explanation: The address ends in verify-account.net. Its owner can place westfield.edu at the start of the address to resemble the school's site.

mod_02.text:
A suspicious bank text contains a phone number and says:

"Call this number immediately if this transaction wasn't yours."

What is the strongest verification method?
options: Ignore the supplied number and use the number from the official banking app, card, or website
Call the number in the text because it claims to be fraud support
Reply to the text first
Search the phone number inside the message
mod_02.explanation: The sender controls the number printed in the text. Dialing the number on your bank card lets you choose who receives the call.

mod_02.text: Which feature is common across fake delivery texts, fake wallet warnings, prize texts, and account-suspension texts?
options: They always contain shortened URLs
They always ask directly for money
They use a message to create trust, fear, urgency, or temptation so the victim takes an unsafe action
They always impersonate a bank
mod_02.explanation: The stories differ, but each gives you a reason to trust the text and follow its instructions. Check the claim independently before acting.

mod_03.text: Which situation is the strongest example of vishing?
options: An unexpected caller claims to be your bank and asks you to read a one-time code
A website displays a fake login page
An email contains a suspicious attachment
A stranger leaves a USB drive in a hallway
mod_03.explanation: The caller borrows the bank's identity and asks for a secret during a voice call. Sharing the code could give them access to the account.

mod_03.text:
A caller says:

"This is your bank's fraud desk. A ₱12,000 transfer is pending. Read me the 6-digit code we just sent so I can cancel it."

What should you do?
options: Read the code because the caller is trying to stop fraud
Give only part of the code
Do not give the code; hang up and contact the bank independently
Ask the caller to repeat your account number first
mod_03.explanation: The code may approve a transaction or login. End the call and check the transfer with the fraud team using your bank's own contact details.

mod_03.text:
Your phone displays "WESTFIELD REGISTRAR" when someone calls.

What does this prove?
options: The caller definitely works for the school
Very little; caller ID information can be spoofed or manipulated
The phone company verified the caller
The call is legitimate if the caller knows your name
mod_03.explanation: Caller ID can show a forged school name. Use the registrar's published number to confirm who contacted you.

mod_03.text: What is the safest way to verify an unexpected bank call?
options: Ask the caller more security questions
Call the number shown in your recent-call list
Ask the caller to send you a text
Hang up and dial the bank using a number from your card or official app
mod_03.explanation: When you dial a number from your card or official app, you choose the destination independently of the incoming caller.

mod_03.text:
A caller claiming to be your bank knows the last four digits of a card you actually own.

What should you conclude?
options: They have proven they work for the bank
Knowing one true detail does not prove the caller's identity
The call is safe unless they ask for your password
Only bank employees can know partial card information
mod_03.explanation: Partial card numbers can appear on receipts or in leaked records. Knowing those digits alone does not authenticate a caller.

mod_03.text:
A caller says:

"Do not hang up. If you disconnect, we cannot stop the transaction."

What is the safest response?
options: Hang up and independently contact the real organization
Stay on the line until the problem is fixed
Give the caller basic information but no password
Put the call on speaker and ask a friend
mod_03.explanation: Keeping you on the line prevents an independent check. You can hang up and ask the real bank whether a transaction is pending.

mod_03.text: Why might a scammer ask you to read a one-time code aloud?
options: To check whether your phone works
To identify your mobile network
To create a support ticket
The code may allow them to approve a login, payment, or account change
mod_03.explanation: The code proves control of your phone to the service that issued it. A scammer can enter it into a login or payment screen while you speak.

mod_03.text:
Campus IT calls and says:

"Your account is logged in from another city. Stay on the line and read the code that just arrived."

What should you do?
options: Read the code if they know your student number
Ask for their employee ID, then continue
Hang up and contact campus IT using the school's known contact information
Wait for another code and give them that one instead
mod_03.explanation: The caller is asking for a code while keeping you on the line. Your school's IT directory gives you a separate route to check the login alert.

mod_03.text: Which situation provides the strongest reason to trust a support call?
options: The caller knows your full name
You initiated the call yourself using an independently verified official number
The correct company name appears on caller ID
The caller knows information about your account
mod_03.explanation: Using an independently verified number puts you in control of whom you call. A familiar voice or a caller ID label offers less assurance.

mod_03.text:
A caller says:

"Act now. Don't hang up and don't tell anyone in the room."

Why is this especially suspicious?
options: Legitimate companies never make phone calls
Real employees cannot discuss account problems
Calls lasting several minutes are usually scams
Urgency and isolation reduce your chance to stop and independently verify the claim
mod_03.explanation: The deadline cuts down your thinking time, and the demand for secrecy cuts off help. Ending the call gives you a chance to verify the story.

mod_03.text: Which sequence most closely matches the vishing playbook taught in the lesson?
options: Borrow a trusted identity → mention a true detail → prevent callback → request a secret/code
Send malware → encrypt files → demand payment → delete backups
Leave a USB → wait for someone to connect it → install malware
Create a fake website → advertise it → wait for search traffic
mod_03.explanation: The role and true detail build trust. Blocking a callback keeps you talking until the caller can ask for the code.

mod_03.text:
A caller appears as your bank's real name, knows your name and partial card number, and describes a purchase you recently made. They then ask you to stay on the line and read a code.

What is the strongest conclusion?
options: The accurate information proves the caller is legitimate
It is safe because the caller only wants a temporary code
The known details do not prove identity; the code request and refusal to let you verify independently are major warning signs
The call is legitimate if the transaction amount is correct
mod_03.explanation: A real purchase detail makes the story convincing. The demand for a code and the attempt to block a callback are stronger reasons to stop.

mod_03.text:
A caller claiming to be from your bank says:

"You can call us back, but only using the number currently shown on your screen."

What should you do?
options: Call that number because it matches caller ID
Ask the caller to call again later
Save the displayed number before hanging up
Ignore the supplied number and use an independently known official number
mod_03.explanation: The number on your screen came from the incoming call and can be spoofed. Look up the number in your banking app or on your card.

mod_03.text:
A caller claiming to be your registrar gives you a believable ticket number and correctly states your course. They insist your enrollment will be cancelled unless you verify immediately.

What is the strongest next step?
options: Give limited information because they know your course
End the call and verify the issue through the registrar's official contact channel
Ask the caller to tell you another private fact
Stay connected while opening the school portal
mod_03.explanation: A ticket number and course name can be copied or invented. Check your enrollment through the registrar's published contact before acting.

mod_03.text: What feature best connects fake bank calls, fake school IT calls, and fake registrar calls?
options: They always use the same phone number
They always ask directly for money
They borrow trust and pressure the victim to say or approve something before independently checking
They always use threatening language
mod_03.explanation: Each caller borrows a familiar role to make an unexpected request sound routine. A separate call to the real organization tests the claim.

mod_04.text: Which situation is the strongest example of pretexting?
options: A website automatically downloads malware
Someone guesses your password repeatedly
A text contains a shortened link
A stranger invents a believable work role and story to convince you to unlock a restricted room
mod_04.explanation: Pretexting starts with a believable role and story that makes an unusual request sound authorized. Look for what that story asks you to do.

mod_04.text:
A visitor with a clipboard says:

"I'm from Facilities. We're doing a surprise key audit."

What should you remember?
options: A clipboard proves they are working
Their appearance and story do not prove their identity or authorization
Surprise audits never happen
Facilities workers never enter buildings
mod_04.explanation: A clipboard makes an audit look official, but the school can check whether it scheduled the visit and what access it approved.

mod_04.text:
A person claiming to be from Facilities asks you to unlock a staff closet and wait outside while they inspect it.

What is the safest response?
options: Do not unlock it until their identity and authorization are verified
Unlock it but remain nearby
Ask whether the inspection will take long
Let them enter if they know the building name
mod_04.explanation: Unlocking the closet would give the visitor unsupervised access. Ask the responsible staff member to verify the visit before opening it.

mod_04.text:
Someone says they are the dean's new assistant and asks you to approve a payment because the dean is currently in a meeting.

What should you do?
options: Approve it because the dean is unavailable
Approve a smaller amount first
Wait and verify the request directly with the dean or authorized process
Ask the assistant to promise the request is legitimate
mod_04.explanation: The dean's absence is being used to bypass payment approval. Wait for confirmation through the school's usual payment process.

mod_04.text:
A visitor says:

"I'm with the accreditation team. Your professor already knows. She stepped out, so copy the class list from her laptop before she returns."

What is the strongest warning sign?
options: Accreditation teams visit schools
The story uses the professor's absence to justify accessing something you normally should not
The visitor did not wear a uniform
Class lists contain student names
mod_04.explanation: The visitor uses the professor's absence as permission to copy private records. Only an authorized person or process can grant that access.

mod_04.text:
A supposed administrator says:

"Do not contact the dean. She's presenting right now and will be upset if this payment is delayed."

Why is this suspicious?
options: Administrators never handle payments
Meetings cannot last long
Payments cannot be made on phones
The story discourages independent verification while creating pressure to comply
mod_04.explanation: Discouraging contact with the dean removes the easiest way to check the payment. The threat of delay pressures you to skip that check.

mod_04.text:
A stranger claims to be helping your professor and asks you to copy a student list from the professor's unattended laptop.

What should you do?
options: Refuse and wait for the professor or another authorized person to confirm the request
Copy only student names
Open the laptop but do not send anything
Ask the stranger whether the data is confidential
mod_04.explanation: The class list contains student information. An unattended laptop and a stranger's explanation give you no authority to share it.

mod_04.text: Which situation gives the strongest evidence that a person is authorized?
options: They know the building name
They carry a clipboard and wear professional clothes
Their identity and access request can be checked through an established school process
They know the name of your professor
mod_04.explanation: An established school process can verify both who the visitor is and what they are allowed to access. A badge alone answers neither question.

mod_04.text:
A visitor says:

"The inspection slot closes in ten minutes. If we miss it, your department will fail the audit."

What role does this statement play in a pretexting attack?
options: It proves an official inspection exists
It verifies the visitor's authority
It protects the department from delays
It creates urgency so you are less likely to stop and verify
mod_04.explanation: The threat of a failed audit makes an artificial deadline feel costly. A real inspection can still be checked with the office that arranged it.

options: A verified employee asks you to walk with them to a shared room
A visitor asks you to unlock a restricted room and leave them alone inside
A coworker waits while you use your own badge
A staff member asks where the copy room is
mod_04.explanation: Leaving a visitor alone in a restricted room gives them access beyond your supervision. Confirm their authorization with the room's custodian first.

mod_04.text: Which sequence most closely matches the pretexting pattern taught in the lesson?
options: Borrow a trusted role → make the trusted person unavailable → request an unusual favor → add time pressure
Send malware → encrypt files → demand payment → erase backups
Call repeatedly → guess a password → lock the account
Offer a prize → ask the victim to install software
mod_04.explanation: The trusted role makes the favor sound routine. Making the approver unavailable and adding a deadline discourages you from checking it.

mod_04.text:
A visitor knows your dean's name, carries a professional badge, and says the dean already approved a vendor payment. The dean is conveniently unavailable, and the visitor wants you to approve it on their phone immediately.

What is the strongest conclusion?
options: Knowing the dean's name proves the story is probably legitimate
The badge is enough if it looks professional
The combination of borrowed authority, an unavailable decision-maker, unusual payment request, and urgency strongly suggests pretexting
The payment is safe if the amount is small
mod_04.explanation: The visitor combines a borrowed identity with a missing approver and a rushed payment. Verify the payment through the school's own process.

mod_04.text:
Someone claiming to be from an accrediting team gives you their name, department, and a believable explanation for accessing a staff laptop.

What is the strongest next step?
options: Let them use the laptop while you watch
Verify the visit through a trusted school contact before allowing access
Ask them one more question about the school
Let them proceed if their story is detailed
mod_04.explanation: A name, department and plausible task can all be rehearsed. A trusted school contact can confirm the visit and the approved access.

mod_04.text:
A visitor claims they need access to a locked drawer while the adviser is away. They say:

"The adviser already knows. Please don't message them yet because we're on a deadline."

What should you do?
options: Open the drawer but stay nearby
Give them only the documents they request
Ask them to return the documents afterward
Refuse to open it until the adviser or another authorized person independently confirms the request
mod_04.explanation: The deadline is being used to keep you from asking the person responsible for the drawer. Keep it locked until you have independent confirmation.

mod_04.text: What feature best connects fake Facilities audits, fake accreditation visits, and fake executive-assistant requests?
options: They always involve physical keys
They always request money
They create a believable role and situation designed to make you bypass normal verification or access rules
They always require the real employee to leave the building
mod_04.explanation: The audit, accreditation visit and payment request each supply a story that makes breaking an access rule seem like part of your job.

mod_05.text: Which situation is the strongest example of baiting?
options: A caller pretends to be your bank
A message threatens to close your account
A USB labeled "Final Exam Answers" is left where students are likely to find it
Someone repeatedly guesses your password
mod_05.explanation: The label promises something students want to see. That curiosity is what may persuade someone to connect an unknown device.

mod_05.text:
You find a USB labeled "Grades 2026" in the computer lab.

What should you do?
options: Do not plug it in; turn it over to the appropriate staff
Plug it into a school computer instead of your own
Open it only long enough to find the owner
Take it home and scan it first
mod_05.explanation: Plugging in the drive exposes the computer before you know what it contains. Staff can handle unknown media through the school's process.

mod_05.text:
A booth outside campus gives students free flash drives and says:

"Plug it in now to claim the files we included."

What is the main security concern?
options: Free flash drives usually have little storage
School computers may not recognize the drive
Students might lose the drive
The free item could be bait containing malicious files or software
mod_05.explanation: An attacker can preload a giveaway drive with harmful files. The instruction to plug it in turns the free gift into a reason to take the risk.

mod_05.text:
A website offers a free cracked version of expensive school software.

Why is downloading it risky?
options: Free software cannot run on modern computers
The installer may contain malware hidden behind the attractive free offer
Cracked programs are always slower
Schools automatically delete every free program
mod_05.explanation: A modified installer can run unwanted software alongside the app you wanted. The free offer encourages you to overlook its source.

mod_05.text:
A hallway poster says:

"FREE CAMPUS WI-FI — Scan this QR code to connect."

What is the safest response?
options: Scan it because the poster is inside the school
Ask a friend to scan it first
Use the school's known Wi-Fi instructions or official portal instead of the unknown QR code
Scan it only if your phone has antivirus software
mod_05.explanation: A QR code can conceal a destination or be pasted over a real poster. The school's own connection instructions provide a known route to its network.

mod_05.text:
You receive a file named:

FreeMovie.mp4.exe

What is the strongest warning sign?
options: The filename is too long
The final .exe means it is an executable program, not simply a video
Movies cannot be downloaded
.mp4 files are always malicious
mod_05.explanation: The last extension is .exe. The earlier .mp4 makes the file resemble a movie, but opening it can execute a program.

mod_05.text:
A pop-up says:

"Congratulations! You won a new phone. Download PrizeClaim.exe now."

What is the safest conclusion?
options: The prize may be bait designed to make you run an unsafe file
The prize is legitimate if the page uses school colors
The offer is safe if no password is requested
Winning a phone online is always impossible
mod_05.explanation: The promised phone gives you a reason to run PrizeClaim.exe. Running the file gives the program a chance to act before you can verify the prize.

mod_05.text:
A classmate finds a USB labeled "Answer Key" and says:

"We can test it on an old laptop first."

What is the best response?
options: Use the old laptop because nothing important is stored there
Scan the USB first, then open it
Copy only the PDF files
Do not plug unknown media into any device just to discover what is inside
mod_05.explanation: An old laptop can still hold data or connect to other devices. Testing the drive yourself exposes that computer to the same unknown contents.

options: Your school provides software through its official student portal
A teacher posts a file in the official learning system
An unknown site promises a "free premium license" if you download and run its installer
A verified store offers a normal student discount
mod_05.explanation: The free license is the lure. The unknown site's installer would run with the permissions of the person opening it.

mod_05.text:
You urgently need to charge your phone and see an unfamiliar public USB charging station.

What is the safer choice when possible?
options: Connect because charging cables cannot transfer data
Use your own charger/power source or another trusted charging method
Connect only for five minutes
Unlock the phone while charging so you can monitor it
mod_05.explanation: Some USB connections carry data as well as power. Using your own power bank or wall charger avoids an unfamiliar data connection.

mod_05.text: Why might an attacker leave several attractive USB drives around a school?
options: To increase the chance that curiosity or temptation causes someone to plug one into a device
To give students free storage
To test whether USB ports work
To identify students who lose property
mod_05.explanation: Several drives create more opportunities for someone to take the bait. An attractive label supplies the motivation to plug one in.

mod_05.text:
A USB labeled "Scholarship Applicants — Confidential" is found outside the registrar's office. It looks new and has the school logo printed on it.

What is the strongest conclusion?
options: The school logo proves it belongs to the registrar
It is safer because it was found near an office
You may open it if you disconnect from Wi-Fi first
The label, location, and logo may all be part of the bait; do not plug it in and report it appropriately
mod_05.explanation: A school logo and a spot near the registrar make the drive look misplaced there on purpose. Hand it to staff without connecting it.

mod_05.text:
A post says:

"Download the leaked answer key before it gets deleted."

The file comes from an unknown file-sharing account.

Why is this dangerous?
options: Answer keys are always fake
Curiosity and scarcity are being used to persuade you to download an untrusted file
File-sharing services cannot contain school files
Deleted files cannot contain malware
mod_05.explanation: The threat that the answer key will disappear makes you rush. The unverified account still controls the file you would open.

mod_05.text: Which situation gives the strongest reason to trust a software download?
options: The website says "100% virus free"
Thousands of people supposedly downloaded it
The software is obtained from the school's official portal or the vendor's independently verified official source
The installer filename matches the product name
mod_05.explanation: Starting at a verified school or vendor site gives you a way to establish who supplied the installer before running it.

mod_05.text: What feature best connects a found "Grades" USB, a free cracked application, an unknown prize QR code, and a "you won a phone" download?
options: They all require USB ports
They all steal passwords immediately
They all depend on school computers
They use something attractive, useful, or interesting to persuade the victim to perform a risky action
mod_05.explanation: Each offer puts a tempting reward in front of a risky step, such as plugging in media, scanning a code or running a download.
